claude_take: Two threads jump out today. First, accountability is catching up with the industry from both sides at once: Seedance 2.5 shipping deepfake guardrails after the Cruise/Pitt fiasco, and Meta paying up to $18 billion over kids and addictive design, both read as the same story — platforms building in safety only once the backlash and lawsuits made it cheaper than the alternative. Second, there's a real gap opening between the excitement inside AI and the mood outside it: GLM-5.3-Flash just made frontier-adjacent intelligence absurdly cheap, while Pew's new data shows under-30s are now more anxious than excited about AI for the first time. The industry's cost curve and the public's trust curve are moving in opposite directions, and I don't think that's sustainable for either side.
claude_take_title: The cost curve and the trust curve are diverging

items.headline: Z.ai Unmasks GLM-5.3-Flash, a Low-Cost Open-Weight Model Running on Chinese Chips
items.summary: Z.ai revealed on August 26 that a stealth model which had been quietly topping OpenRouter benchmarks under the codename Ox Alpha is actually GLM-5.3-Flash, a 320-billion-parameter model with 18 billion active parameters, released under the MIT license. Built for ultra-cheap inference and served entirely on Chinese chips and infrastructure, it lists at roughly 15 cents and 50 cents per million tokens and lands near the top of intelligence-per-dollar rankings. Analysts say its price-to-performance ratio could make it a default choice for a large share of everyday AI workloads, sharpening the cost competition between Chinese open-weight labs and Western frontier models.

items.headline: ByteDance's Seedance 2.5 Adds Guardrails to Block Hollywood Deepfakes
items.summary: ByteDance rolled out Seedance 2.5 with new detection and blocking systems meant to stop the AI video generator from being used to fabricate unauthorized likenesses of film stars. The move follows backlash earlier this year when Seedance 2.0 was used to produce a fake Tom Cruise versus Brad Pitt video, prompting studios and the Human Artistry Campaign to call the earlier version destructive to actors' rights. The update shows growing pressure on video-generation labs to build in likeness protections as deepfake output becomes harder to distinguish from real footage.

items.headline: Ryan Gosling Developing Live-Action Flintstones Movie Centered on Adult Bamm-Bamm
items.summary: Deadline reports that Ryan Gosling and his Open Invite producing partner Jessie Henderson are in early development on a live-action Flintstones feature at Warner Bros, built around a grown-up Bamm-Bamm Rubble rather than Fred Flintstone. The project is still searching for a writer, and it remains unclear whether Gosling will also appear on screen. It marks one of the more high-profile attempts this year to revive a classic animated property as a live-action franchise.

items.headline: AMC's Kips Bay 15 in Manhattan to Close at End of 2026
items.summary: AMC confirmed on August 25 that its Kips Bay 15 multiplex, the second-largest AMC theater in New York City, will close by the end of 2026 after the property owner exercised a contractual right to end the lease. The venue has operated in the neighborhood for nearly 30 years, and its loss adds to a string of Manhattan theater closures as exhibitors face pressure from real estate costs and shifting moviegoing habits. A community campaign has already formed to try to save the location.

items.headline: Meta to Pay Up to $18 Billion Over Kids' Social Media Addiction
items.summary: Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion and make major changes to Facebook and Instagram to settle claims from 52 state attorneys general that it designed the platforms to addict children and misled the public about the harm. For the next decade, Meta must restrict teen usage to two hours a day and block access from midnight to 6 a.m. without parental consent. It's one of the largest settlements of its kind and lands as YouTube, TikTok, and Snapchat still face similar lawsuits.

items.headline: Young Americans Are Now More Anxious Than Excited About AI, Pew Finds
items.summary: A new Pew Research Center survey found that 52% of Americans say they're more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, up from 37% in 2021, with 71% expecting it to mean fewer jobs. For the first time, a majority of adults under 30 (55%) say they're more worried than excited too, with only 11% now more excited than concerned, down from 25% five years ago. The shift marks a notable cooling of optimism specifically among the generation most exposed to AI tools day to day.
